summary:
JezeroTrace is an open-source web cockpit for planning a human spacewalk (EVA) at Jezero Crater, Mars. It answers the three questions a crew asks before going outside: where to go, how to get there, and why the map can be trusted. It combines a slope layer and hillshade built from the USGS HiRISE terrain model (1 m/pixel) with a CTX image background, four science points of interest, and least-cost walking routes limited by slope. What makes it different is that every layer carries a data card stating its source, version, resolution, license and known issues. 

We also check our route logic against the path actually driven by the Perseverance rover, using parameters locked before the comparison, and we report the result as it is. Everything is reproducible from public NASA data and released under Apache 2.0.
details:
JezeroTrace: A Map That Shows Its Sources

A slope map looks precise. But it hides the resolution of its source, its version, its license and the artifacts of the instrument that made it. For a crew about to walk across Mars, a map they cannot question is a risk. JezeroTrace is built on one idea: a planning display is only as good as the evidence it shows next to the picture.

What is JezeroTrace?

General-purpose Mars viewers are built mostly for regional and global views. They are not built for the small area one astronaut covers in a single EVA. JezeroTrace is an EVA-scale planning view of Jezero Crater, built for mission planners, crew trainers, students, and teams who want to reuse an open pipeline from public Mars data to web layers. Its aim is to help plan walks to places of geological interest. In this prototype the four points of interest are a cliff edge, a plateau, a crater and a cone, picked by eye from the hillshade image.

Features That Define the Cockpit

Where to go. Four points of interest, chosen by eye from the hillshade image. They are not CRISM detections, and the page never claims that spectra chose them.

How to get there. Four pre-computed least-cost walking routes from the landing area to each point, computed from the slope raster with a slope constraint only. Each route shows its length and maximum slope. Spectral data play no role in cost.

Why you can trust it. Every layer has a data card with its source mission and instrument, version, resolution, license and known issues. For example, the terrain layer is the USGS HiRISE DTM mosaic, version 006, 1 m/pixel, CC0 1.0 (DOI 10.5066/P9REJ9JN), and its card lists stereo DTM artifacts and seams, and the east-west slope limit described below. The origin and limits of each picture are one click away.

Honest labels. The page states that it shows a static data snapshot, not live data, and it states the coordinate system.

How It Works

  1. We download the Jezero HiRISE terrain mosaic and the CTX mosaic, and crop both to a 4 km by 4 km study area.
  2. We compute slope from elevation differences between neighbouring pixels, and make a hillshade from the same terrain model.
  3. Layers are exported as image overlays and listed in a layers.json file, which the page reads to build its layer list.
  4. Routing code finds the lowest-cost path under a slope limit. All parameters are stored in a configuration file.
  5. A GitHub Actions workflow publishes the page. It reads only pre-computed files, so there is no server to run.

Checked Against the Real Rover

We compared our route logic with the path actually driven by the Perseverance rover. This is a sanity check, not proof that our routes are best and not a safety validation. Distances are computed in a local azimuthal equidistant projection on a sphere of radius 3,396,190 m, because the terrain model's map metres are not true ground distances away from latitude 0. The comparison parameters were committed to validation/params.json before any comparison was run, and the routing code has automated tests.

Result: we ran our route finder once, from the first point to the last point of the first Perseverance path segment inside our map (899 reference points, about 1,271 m of rover path). Our route is 727 m long. The overlap score M1 is 0.15 at a 10 m tolerance, a weak match under the thresholds we set in advance (below 0.50). The median distance between the two paths is 34.28 m and the 95th percentile is 127.30 m. We did not change any parameter after seeing this. The four routes shown on the website were not part of this comparison.

What We Chose Not to Claim

We prefer a smaller claim that is true to a larger one that is not. We did not build a spectral (CRISM) layer, a boulder or hazard layer, or radiation and dust models. Points of interest were placed by hand, not by a repeatable rule. We also found that we used 1 m pixel spacing in both directions, while the true east-west ground spacing is about 0.95 m, so east-west gradients are understated by about 5%. We documented this effect instead of risking a late change.

Our Mission: Planning With Evidence

Future surface crews will need tools that tell them not only what the terrain looks like, but how much to trust it. JezeroTrace shows that this habit can be built into a map from the start, by a team of beginners, with open data and open code.

Impact

  • Planners and trainers: an EVA-scale view where the origin and limits of every layer sit next to the picture, so people can judge how far to trust a route.
  • Learners: a complete, documented example of turning public NASA data into a decision map. The documentation shows the steps and the mistakes, not only the result.
  • Other teams: an open pipeline and a data-card format that others can copy for their own layers.

We do not claim measured user numbers or adoption. This is what we intend, and what a viewer can check on the live page today.

Future

Next: recompute slope with the true east-west spacing and re-run validation with the same locked parameters; turn CRISM hydrous mineral detections into a documented layer with its own data card; write a repeatable rule for choosing points; validate against more Perseverance segments; add a boulder and hazard layer.

Later: show radiation and dust context where coverage and license allow; test the page with people who work in planetary surface operations; reuse the pipeline for other landing sites.

Longer term: automatically pick up new HiRISE and CTX products; invite others to contribute data cards; ask planetary geologists to review our points and known-issue notes.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

The finished product does not call an AI model. It is a static website, and every layer and route is computed in advance by ordinary code. AI was used in our development process: Kiro with Claude models, and Claude in chat for planning, drafting and proofreading English. AI tools were also used to make the illustrative footage in our demo video (the Mars globe, the astronaut scenes and the concept scenes). That footage is labelled as AI-generated on screen, and it shows ideas, not features of the website.

AI helped write and revise pipeline, routing, validation and web code, and draft documentation. We chose the science goal, data, scope and points of interest. We gave the AI written rules: never invent a number, record the source and version of every figure, and compute every validation number with code. Team members checked and tested the outputs we kept, and each member kept a log in docs/ai_log/.
